"My Great Master has already entered parinirvāṇa, and now my Upādhyāya has likewise passed away. The Eye of the World is extinguished; I cannot descend again.
He immediately manifested fire to cremate his body, and streams of water flowed from the four directions into Jambudvīpa, amidst the assembly for the compilation of the scriptures.
The monk Śāriputra spoke this verse:

"I, Gavāmpati, bow my head in homage to the Great Virtuous Saṅgha, the most excellent among the wondrous assembly. Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall follow him, just as when a great elephant departs, the elephant calf follows."
Thereupon he entered parinirvāṇa in the heavens.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also speaks in this manner.
Regarding "Piṇḍola Bharadvāja," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

Piṇḍola Bharadvāja is foremost in the ability to roar the lion’s roar. According to the *Biqin-toulu jing* (Sūtra on Inviting Piṇḍola), "Piṇḍola" is his personal name, the meaning of which is not yet fully understood;

"Bharadvāja" is his clan name, which signifies one of sharp faculties. Whenever a new house, bathhouse, vegetarian feast, or new garment is prepared, he should first be invited. Those who wish to invite him should, in a quiet place, burn incense, prostrate, and with a sincere heart call out toward Mount Mālina in the country of India:
"Homage to the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who, having received the Buddha’s command, acts as a field of merit for those in the age of the Dharma's decay; may he accept my invitation."
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: That person originally coveted a sandalwood bowl;

for the sake of the householder Jyotiṣka, he manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to go and take it. The Buddha rebuked him and did not permit him to remain in this realm, whereupon he immediately departed for Aparagoyānī to teach and transform sentient beings.
The *Samyak-saṃbodhi Sūtra* states:

Because the Buddha wished to deliver that king—a difficult-to-transform adherent of the naked ascetics—He caused all His disciples to manifest supernatural transformations and arrive there simultaneously to accept his invitation.

At that time, Piṇḍola was sewing his robes in the mountains and had forgotten to take them with him. Suddenly remembering, he pierced the ground with his needle; the thread was still attached to the robes, so he exercised his supernormal powers and went there immediately. Because the mountain was pulled by the needle and thread, it followed after him.
At that time, there was a pregnant woman in that country who, seeing a great mountain approaching and obscuring the sky, fell into a state of terror and miscarried.
The Buddha, knowing this from afar, commanded Maudgalyāyana to go and say to her:
"What mountain is that behind you?"
Pindola looked back and saw him; he seized this mountain and hurled it eight thousand li away.
The Buddha said to him:
"I have taught all sentient beings so that they might attain nirvana, yet now you have missed the appointed time and killed a person."

"Human life is precious and is something I do not favor. From this day forward, you shall no longer follow me for meals nor participate in my assemblies. I shall keep you as a field of merit for future generations; you shall attain parinirvāṇa only when the Buddha Maitreya appears."
Having heard this, Piṇḍola felt distressed and reproached himself; after finishing his meal, he entered the mountains.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:

"An Arhat who is free from afflictions can, like a Bodhisattva at the eighth stage, cultivate the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and remain in the world for as long as he wishes; thus, Piṇḍola is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and not an actual body."
Regarding "Kālodāyin," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"This name means 'Black Radiance' (*kṛṣṇābha*).
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states:
He was named Kṛṣṇābhāsa.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

Kālodāyin’s body was extremely black. While walking for alms at night, it was pitch dark when he arrived at another’s house. A flash of lightning struck, and the woman of that household, who was then pregnant, saw him in the lightning’s glare and mistook him for a black demon. Terrified, she miscarried, whereupon he said to her:
"What kind of spirit are you?
He replied, "I am a disciple of Gautama; I have come now to beg for alms."
That woman immediately uttered foul abuse.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, commanded the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, you must not eat past midday, nor shall you go begging for food in advance."
“Mahā-Kapphiṇa” means “Lunar Mansion of the Room” (Hángxiù) in this language.

Tradition holds that because he first entered the gateway of the Path while staying overnight in a monastic cell, the Buddha, knowing his roots of virtue were about to ripen, personally transformed himself into an elderly bhikṣu and stayed with him overnight; having preached the Dharma for him, he thereby realized the Noble Path, and was thus named “Lunar Mansion of the Room.”
He is also named Fangxing (Star of the Chamber), as he was born due to prayers offered to the Star of the Chamber; thus this became his name.
"Bakkula" means "Excellent Appearance" (Suyukta-rūpa) in this language, referring to his handsome countenance and dignified demeanor.
In the past, he once observed the single precept of non-killing, and now he has obtained five rewards of immortality:
first, he does not die when boiled in a cauldron;
second, he is not scorched when pressed upon a griddle.
Third, falling into water, one does not drown;
fourth, being swallowed by fish, one is not digested;
fifth, being cut by a blade, one is not wounded.
The *Sūtra on the Former Deeds of the Five Hundred Disciples* states:

"In the past, I once gave medicine to a sick monk and offered a single harītakī fruit to a śramaṇa; for ninety kalpas since then, I have not fallen into the evil realms, and this year, at the age of one hundred and sixty, I have never been ill."
Furthermore, the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-śāstra* states:
"In the past, Bakula was a householder. Once, while intoxicated, he entered a monastery and cried out: 'O Bhikṣus!'"
"If you have need of it, you should come to my home.
The next morning, a bhikṣu came to ask for medicine, saying he suffered from a headache.
The elder said, "This is water above the diaphragm surging upward to attack the head; that is why the head aches."
He immediately gave him a harītakī fruit; after the bhikṣu consumed it, he was cured.

Because of this, for ninety-one kalpas he never suffered from illness. When he reached the age of eighty, he left the household life to study the Way. From then until now, more than eighty years have passed, totaling one hundred and sixty years.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states:

"For more than eighty years, I have worn robes made of discarded rags (pāṃsukūla), yet I do not recall ever having used a needle and thread to sew a garment, nor even a needle-case or a single strand of cotton. I have never begged for alms from a wealthy household, nor have I ever looked upon the face of a woman or entered the quarters of bhikṣuṇīs, nor have I ever conversed with them."

I do not recall ever having kept a single śrāmaṇera; furthermore, I have never suffered even briefly from a headache or similar ailment, nor have I ever taken a single pill of medicine. For eighty years, I have constantly sat in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) without ever leaning against anything.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka traveled everywhere to pay homage to the various stūpas and bestowed precious treasures upon them in abundance. Hearing that Bakula was foremost among those with few desires, he offered him a single coin.
Then the deity of that stupa cast it back out again.
The king said, "Excellent!"

The newly translated *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* is named "Mañjuśrī," while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* names him "Samantabhadra"; there is also a sūtra that names him "Maitreya.

The *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* (瓔珞經), fascicle four, states:

The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states:

as there is no aging or illness in the land, there is no suffering of sickness."

When one's lifespan is about to end, one aspires to be born in the pure lands of the ten directions; being able to be reborn there according to one’s wish is freedom from the suffering of death, which is the cessation of every moment of thought.
Joy and bliss accompany one constantly, so there is no suffering of association with the hated and the disliked.
Since the mind is entirely equanimous and free from enmity, even when parting from those one leaves behind or meeting those who remain, there is no suffering of separation from the beloved.
Their desires are fulfilled according to their wishes; they suffer neither from the pain of unfulfilled seeking nor from the suffering of poverty.

the *Contemplation Sutra* and the *Sutra on Pure Awakening* speak according to the largest scale, ranging from twenty li up to six hundred thousand li. However, these dimensions vary according to one's recollection and thus lack a fixed standard.

However, this sutra mentions only four colors; according to the *Qingjing jue jing* and the *Guan jing*, every petal and leaf is made of various precious colors—why then does it state here that they are exclusively blue with only blue light?

In that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays. This next passage explains the third excellence: the sounding of celestial instruments.
According to the *Sūtra on Contemplation of Amitābha* and other texts, immeasurable musical instruments are constantly suspended in the heavens, sounding spontaneously without being struck.

Furthermore, these instruments are suspended according to the location of beings—whether in houses or forests—and they all resonate harmoniously in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings. They all produce the sounds of the Dharma, with no sound that is not the voice of the Dharma; those among humans and devas who hear them all give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
The Sūtra says:
"The ground is made of gold. This next explains the fourth point: the ground is adorned with *tān-jin* (refined gold), meaning its appearance is perfectly pure and round.
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The lands traversed by Amitāyus Buddha are adorned everywhere with rare wonders.

According to various sutras, the substance of the ground is mostly gold, interspersed with various jewels so that it is transparent both within and without; thus, the *Sūtra on Contemplation of Amitāyus* refers to it as a lapis lazuli ground.
Furthermore, that sutra states:

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
“Those Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwell supported by space.”
The Sūtra says:

The *Treatise on the Infinite Life* (*Wǔliàngshòu lùn*) states:
It is the rain of adornments.

Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:

The flowers covered the ground to a thickness of more than four inches; they were arranged in their respective colors without any confusion, possessing a lustrous sheen and being fragrant and soft. When it rains new flowers once more, the old flowers gradually split open to receive them; thus the old flowers completely disappear and the new flowers fill the space. Or, it may rain precious garments that cover the ground everywhere, which people tread upon as they walk.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Those who behold these flowers experience mental joy, yet they do not become attached to them; furthermore, this increases the sublime merit of sentient beings."

*Mandāra* is translated here as "red round lotus," and is also called "wish-fulfilling flower" (*yìrúihuā*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is named "pleasing flower" (*shìyìhuā*) and "great pleasing flower. *Mañjūṣaka* is named "soft flower" (*róuruǎnhuā*).

To explain this: although the flower arises from the mind, the color and form of the flower ultimately remain red and round; subsequently, the six-feathered bird travels through the various directions.
Question:

yet they travel by means of transporting their bodies or by riding in palaces, why do you speak of 'feathered vehicles'?"
Answer: "It means that his flight is like being borne by wings and his speed is like riding a dragon; hence it is called 'winged carriage' (*yùjià*).
This refers to mounting the perfect purity (*yuánjìng*), meaning to mount the power of great meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and great wisdom (*prajñā*)."
The text further consists of three parts:
first, the offering of flowers while circumambulating; second, the limited morning circuit of the path; and third, the conclusion as the attainment of Sukhāvatī.
The Sūtra says:

"The sentient beings of that land always, at the break of dawn, each take various wonderful flowers in their robes and bowls to make offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions. This next passage explains the first point: the successive offering of flowers held in the hands.

According to various sutras, they may travel by means of palaces made of the seven treasures or lotuses of a hundred jewels, or they may simply depart on their own; or, riding upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they traverse the worlds of the ten directions in a single thought-moment. Before the various Buddhas, they provide diverse offerings according to their mental inclinations, prostrate to the Buddhas, listen to the Dharma, and some even receive predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). "Yige" (衣裓) refers to the lap or the breast of a garment.
The Sūtra says:
"At the very time of eating, he returned to his own country to eat and perform walking meditation. This next passage explains the second restriction regarding the morning circuit.
It means that upon reaching the time for the midday meal at dawn, he immediately returns to his country; this signifies the maintenance of perfect purity.
This means that one sustains the body through the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma; having thus partaken of food and drink, one preaches the Dharma and recites the sūtras.
"Practicing the sūtra" refers to circumambulating while contemplating it.
He asked: "Regarding the time for eating, does it refer to the same period here, namely the interval between noon and mid-afternoon, or is it a different time? He replied:
"Although they differ in length, they are the same in terms of eating.
Question: "Among the four types of nutriment, what kind of nutriment do they have?"
He replied:

"They have solid food, yet they never eat it; seeing forms and smelling fragrances serves as their sustenance. They are naturally satiated and feel no attachment to flavors; once their task is finished, they depart by transformation, returning of their own accord when the time comes."
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"When they wish to eat, bowls and vessels made of the seven precious jewels appear spontaneously before them, filled to the brim with food and drink of a hundred flavors."
As stated in the *Qingjing jue jing* (Sutra on Pure Awakening):

"When one desires to eat, there spontaneously appear karpāsa and kārpāsa-cotton cloths to serve as seats; those who eat sit upon them. All the bodhisattvas and arhats partake of the meal, which is naturally equal—neither too much nor too little—and they do not eat with delight because of its excellence."
"Why are these two sūtras not the same?
He replied:
"Regarding eating and not eating, those who eat do so neither too much nor too little."
If one does not eat, merely seeing it is sufficient; this refers to the land of physical forms (*rūpa*).
As for the land of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The Dharma of ambrosia is the food, and the flavor of liberation is the drink."
The Sūtra says:
"The land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues. This next section explains the third point, establishing the perfection of Ultimate Bliss.

The seventh point clarifies the birds' melodies as the Dharma-sound; this refers to the perfect purity of the retinue. That is to say, within the Pure Land, the Tathāgata manifests various classes of followers—such as devas, nāgas, and the eight divisions of supernatural beings—to demonstrate a retinue of majestic disciples.
Question:
"Is that land included within the three realms?

Although it is said that Mount Sumeru does not exist there, the fact that the six heavens of the desire realm all dwell in the void means they are still subsumed under the desire realm. How then can it be that real animals do not exist there, such that they must be merely emanations?"
Answer: "According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and other texts, it is said to be within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:"
If a transformed land from another direction is mixed with evil and impurity, it is said to be subsumed under the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is pure, it is not subsumed under the three realms; furthermore, because it has form, it is not the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); because it dwells upon the earth, it is not the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and because it is free from desire, it is not the desire realm.

Therefore, although the inhabitants of that land resemble those of the desire realm, they do not belong to the desire realm; consequently, they are not subsumed within the three realms, and there are no actual animals there.
Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"Above the four heavens, there are no actual animals."
"The abodes adorned by the power of the merit of the various devas also have birds and beasts, yet these are not actual retributions; how much less could they exist in the Pure Land!
As for what are called 'birds,' some are emanations of Amitābha, appearing in the form of jewel-light."
This text has two parts:
first, the introduction; second, the explanation that removes external doubts.
The introductory section has five parts:
First, a general indication of the feathered species;
second, a specific enumeration of bird names;
third, the warbling of harmonious and elegant sounds.
Fourth, expounding the wondrous Dharma;
fifth, hearing sounds and stirring thoughts.
As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In that land there are always various wonderful birds of diverse colors. This first sentence provides a general description of the feathered species; they are called "various" because their colors and types are not uniform, and they are called "wonderful" because their appearance is peerless.
The Sūtra says:
"White cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and the saṃjīvaka birds"—this is the second section, which enumerates the names of various birds individually.
The *Buddhāvataṃsaka-acintya-sūtra* states:
"Śāli" means the magpie in this language.
Regarding the *kalaviṅka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

As for the kalaviṅka, it has no formal name in this language and is called the "Fine-Sounding Bird. Although the chick of this bird has not yet emerged from its shell, its voice already surpasses that of all other birds; how much more so once it has emerged!
Regarding the *saṃjīvaka* bird, tradition says it has one body and two heads.
The Sūtra states:
"All these birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, utter harmonious and elegant sounds. This next section explains the third point: the utterance of harmonious and elegant sounds.
The Sūtra says:

"Its voice eloquently expounds the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and so forth. This refers to the sequential and fourfold exposition of the sublime Dharma.
The thirty-seven factors are also called the thirty-seven aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
"Thirty-seven" refers to their number; that is to say, they are thirty-seven mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Regarding the term "categories" (*pakṣa*), it means that because the thirty-seven factors are each distinct, they are called categories.

Regarding the term "aiding the path" (*bodhipakṣika*), it means that they are able to accord with and assist the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), thereby causing the power and function of the Noble Path to become superior; thus, they are called the "two knowledges that aid the path."
If one speaks of *bodhi*, *bodhi* is also termed "awakening" (*jue*), which refers precisely to the two aforementioned types of wisdom.
Thus, the *Catuhsatyaka-śāstra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are the primary study of the Hīnayāna; the Bodhisattva, however, concurrently cultivates both types of wisdom."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
For what reason does the Tathāgata frequently teach this Dharma as being neither increasing nor decreasing, yet speak only of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? Answer:

These thirty-seven factors are like a compounding of various medicines; to cure the illnesses of sentient beings, exactly this many are required. Therefore, it is always said that there are neither more nor fewer.

Furthermore, the term "constant recitation" (smṛti) refers to the sequential names for the initial stages of entering the Path. Just as when a person first arrives at a teacher’s place to hear the Dharma, they first apply their mind to remember and retain what they have heard, it is therefore mindfulness (smṛti) that is clarified first.

Having reflected thus, one acts accordingly; therefore, right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is explained next, consisting of the diligent abandonment of the two evils and the diligent cultivation of the two virtues.

If there is excessive vigor, the mind becomes distracted; wishing to collect the mind so that it abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are explained next.
Once the mind is concentrated, the five faculties (pañcendriya) arise.
As these five faculties gradually increase, they are able to obstruct the afflictions (kleśa) and enter into the profound Dharma; therefore, the five powers (pañcabala) are explained next.
Once the five powers have increased, one is able to discern the Noble Path (āryamārga); therefore, the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) are taught next.

Having already seen the Truths, one must eliminate the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in order to proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa; therefore, the Eightfold Noble Path is explained next.
A detailed analysis is provided in full in a separate chapter.
Question:
"According to what the parrot has explained, one ought to provide a complete exposition; why, then, does the sutra speak of only four categories? Answer:

"However, because the bodies of those born by transformation lack impurities such as pus and blood, they do not harbor inverted attachments regarding the pure or the impure; therefore, mindfulness of the body is not taught for them.
Furthermore, although they lack painful sensations, they also lack mental distortions regarding pleasant retributions; therefore, mindfulness of sensation is not taught."
Knowing in one's heart that all things are impermanent, one exerts sincerity in cultivating the Path; thus, one does not speak of mental recollection.
Knowing that all phenomena are without self, one is free from the inversion of selfhood; thus, one does not speak of dharma-recollection.
For these reasons, one does not speak of the four applications of mindfulness.

Furthermore, because they have never committed evil and are free from afflictions, there is no need to speak of their abandonment; they ardently and self-exertedly cultivate the various noble paths without relying on verbal instruction. Therefore, the birds do not speak of the four right efforts.

Furthermore, because they cultivate both concentration and wisdom and are not constantly distracted, they have attained the five supernormal powers; there is no need to laboriously mention the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda). Therefore, the first three groups of birds do not proclaim [the Dharma].

Furthermore, as for the explanation [of the term "bird"], that interpretation is not correct; the sutra merely provides a brief mention without declaring it to be anything other than a bird. Moreover, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are said to be:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of awakening (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ*).
The four foundations of mindfulness refer to:
body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
The four right efforts refer to:

One employs skillful means to prevent unarisen evil from arising; one employs skillful means to abandon evil that has already arisen; one employs skillful means to give rise to unarisen good; and one employs skillful means to increase good that has already arisen.
The four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are:
the base of concentration through desire, the base of concentration through energy, the base of concentration through mindfulness, and the base of concentration through wisdom.
The five faculties (indriya) are:
The faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
As for the five powers, they are:
the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of wisdom, and the power of concentration.
The seven factors of enlightenment are:

the enlightenment factor of discrimination of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of concentration.
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
The essential nature consists of ten factors, namely:
pure faith, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, as well as joy, tranquility, equanimity associated with the factors of enlightenment, equanimity, volition, ethical discipline, and concentration.
The factor of faith is twofold, namely:
the faculty of faith and the power of faith.
The factor of diligence is eightfold, namely:
The four right efforts are fourfold:
the faculty of energy, the power of energy, the factor of enlightenment of energy, and right effort;
mindfulness is divided into four, namely:
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
The category of wisdom is eightfold, namely the four foundations of mindfulness as four:
the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, and right view.

Joy is the factor of enlightenment of joy; tranquility is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; equanimity is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; volition is a factor of enlightenment; and reckoning is called right intention.
Morality is divided into three, namely:
right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Regarding samādhi-concentration, concentration is divided into eight factors: namely, the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda) constitute four;
these are the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration.
Question: "For what reason are they called 'dharmas that assist the path'?
What is the meaning of 'assisting the path'?"

He replied: "The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are enlightenment (*bodhi*). Because these various dharmas accord with those [knowledges] and cause their power and function to become superior, they are called the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)."
The Sūtra says:

"When the sentient beings in that land hear this sound, they all bring to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. This refers to the successive hearing of sounds that moves the mind; that is to say, upon hearing the birds preaching the Dharma, they all give rise to wholesome thoughts and bring the Three Jewels to mind.
Question:
"Many sūtras frequently speak of the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti); why does this one alone mention only three? Answer:

Regarding the "six recollections," one teaches these six recollections based on this realm and the lower realms: because sentient beings lack the full faculties and have obtained bodies in the evil destinies, one teaches them to recollect the precepts (*śīla-smṛti*) so that they may uphold the precepts;
because sentient beings are impoverished and destitute, one teaches them to recollect giving (*dāna-smṛti*) so that they may abandon stinginess;
and because those in the lower realms do not reach the status of devas, one intends for them to cultivate celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*), and thus causes them to recollect the devas (*deva-smṛti*).

Because the sentient beings in that land have no evil destinies, they naturally cultivate goodness and thus do not think of precepts; because there is no defilement of violating the precepts, they do not think of them.

Because there are none who suffer from poverty, they do not think of giving; yet they still hold flowers and scatter them before all Buddhas—this is an offering, not giving—and because those sentient beings lack the defilement of stinginess, they do not think of giving.
Because the physical forms and the environments of those people surpass those of the Sixth Heaven, they do not think of the heavens.
Because the field of merit of the Triple Gem is supreme and peerless, one should simply be mindful of the Triple Gem.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

A blind bandit regained his faculty of sight by being mindful of the Buddha; the daughter of King Śreṇika had her hands and feet restored by being mindful of the Buddha; merchants were immediately freed from the peril of fish-eaters by being mindful of the Buddha; and Mahāsena was relieved of the pain of his sores by being mindful of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"One thought-moment of Amitābha Buddha removes the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
To utter "Namo Buddha" even once, one shall all attain the path of Buddhahood;
this is the power of mindfulness of the Buddha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
By recollecting the *prajñāpāramitā*, one eliminates the four hundred and four diseases, leaves behind calamities and disasters, and eradicates all evil karma;
or by recollecting the various *samādhis*, one attains superior knowledge and vision.
This is the power of mindfulness of the Dharma.
If a person mindfully recollects Avalokiteśvara, Kṣitigarbha, or Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva, all calamities will be eliminated and their aspirations will be fulfilled.
"This is the power of mindfulness of the Sangha.
Question: "The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says:"
All phenomena are ultimately empty by nature; within this emptiness, there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Sangha.
If one were to speak of or conceive of forms and characteristics as being worthy of mindfulness, that would constitute a perversion.
"How should one maintain mindfulness? He replied:
"If that sutra is based on the principle of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), this present sutra is based on the method of gradual guidance, proceeding from the shallow to the profound."

Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment practices mindfulness of the Buddha, they should first mindfully contemplate the form-body (*rūpakāya*). They should contemplate the Buddha of the form-body by means of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. When the mind gradually attains entry into the profound Dharma, one should contemplate the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) Buddha. As one subsequently enters even deeper and attains superior power, one should contemplate by means of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), not by means of the form-body, nor should one be attached to the Dharma-body. Because one well knows that all phenomena are eternally quiescent like empty space, there is nothing to be contemplated and no one who contemplates; this is true mindfulness. However, for those who have newly resolved their minds, we now provide mindfulness by way of phenomenal characteristics."
As the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"There are seven superior qualities of the Buddha for which one should maintain mindfulness:
first, his body is superior, because he is fully endowed with all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)."
Second is the excellence of abiding in accordance with the Dharma, because his three types of action are always free from error;
third is the excellence of wisdom, because he possesses the knowledge of all modes;
fourth is the excellence of fulfillment, because all his merits are perfected.
The excellence of the five elements is due to their constant abiding in samādhi;
the excellence of the six inconceivables is due to the full possession of the six supernormal powers;
and the excellence of the seven liberations is due to the complete exhaustion of all afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The Buddha has three bodies; when a bodhisattva practices the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), which body should they take as their object? Answer:

"Contemplating the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), although the Dharma-body possesses immeasurable and profound principles, one should practice *buddhānusmṛti* (recollection of the Buddha) by way of seven aspects of the Dharma-body.
These seven aspects are the primary functions of the Dharma-body and are also its perfect virtues: 1. The Perfect Virtue of Equal Benefit for All Beings:

This refers to the ability to manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that achieve enlightenment and perform great benefit—causing those bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings who have not yet planted the seeds [of liberation] to plant them; causing those who are not yet matured to reach maturity; and causing those who are not yet liberated to attain liberation."

Second, the perfection of being free from faults: because both the cognitive and afflictive obstructions have been eternally extinguished and abandoned, there are no afflictions that could give rise to faults.
Third, the perfection of non-obstruction: by virtue of wisdom, one’s mind is not obstructed by joy or sorrow regarding the eight worldly concerns.

Fourth, the perfection of being able to bestow the great joy of the Dharma: because one possesses both internal and external wealth, one constantly experiences abundant happiness; furthermore, one attains a pure land where one personally enjoys the joy of the Dharma, and also enables the bodhisattvas of other regions to enjoy the joy of the Dharma.

Fifth, the perfection of effortlessness (*anābhoga*) means that all activities are spontaneously accomplished by the Tathāgata without effort; because of the power of his original vows, whatever he intends to do is accomplished naturally.

According to that treatise, it is the same as the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra*; thus, that treatise states:

These two treatises take the first bhūmi as the stage of non-retrogression.
Thus, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra* asks:
"What is non-retrogression?"
Answer:

Because all Bodhisattvas have attained the cause of definitive certainty in the first stage (*bhūmi*), they abandon the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions through the power of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), just like a *srotāpanna*.

By severing the causes of regression that are contrary to the bodhicitta and abandoning afflictions such as the view of a self, one is then designated as having entered the rank of a Bodhisattva; one personally knows and realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness, thereby transcending the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
At that time, there are nine kinds of perfections:
first, the perfection of entering the stage, meaning one initially enters the bodhisattva stage because one has for the first time attained the supramundane mind;
second, the perfection of family, meaning one is born into the family of the Buddhas because one is born by relying on the wisdom of prajñā.
Third, the excellence of lineage (*gotra*), because it is born from the practice of the Mahāyāna and its noble lineage is beyond reproach;
fourth, the excellence of emergence (*niryāṇa*), because it cannot be subsumed by any worldly path;
fifth, the excellence of entry (*praveśa*), because one enters the supramundane path and its dharmas.
Sixth, the transcendence of the body, because one abides well within the Dharma of the bodhisattva, taking great compassion as its essence;
seventh, the transcendence of place, because one abides well in the locus of the bodhisattva’s correct practice, neither abandoning the world nor being defiled by it;

eighth, the transcendence of activity, which refers to entering the true suchness (tathatā) that is equal throughout the three periods of time, and giving rise to a life that accords with the noble wisdom of emptiness through the semblance of dharmas.

9. Ultimate transcendence (*atyantadoṣa*): This means entering into the lineage of the Tathāgata so as to ensure that the Buddha-lineage is not interrupted, because one ultimately realizes the path to nirvāṇa.
Thus, the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) is located in the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).

According to the *Saṃbhāra-śāstra*, when a bodhisattva attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they immediately abide in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) and will certainly become a Buddha without ever regressing.
Thus, the stage of non-retrogression resides in the eighth bhūmi.
Therefore, he himself poses the question:

"For what reason is it that from the first bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi, although all are definitely directed toward *sambodhi*, they are not called 'non-retrogressive,' whereas only those dwelling in the Immovable Bhūmi are so designated?"
Answer:

The supramundane roots of goodness, such as faith and so forth, possessed by a Bodhisattva on the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi) cannot be obstructed or caused to regress by Bodhisattvas of the seventh ground or by those of the two vehicles; therefore, that ground is called "Non-retrogression" (Avivartika).
If one were to judge by those sentient beings who are born there and reach the seventh or eighth stage, their status would be far too high;
if they reach the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), it accords with the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. Thus that sūtra says:
"Sentient beings born there may, after one kalpa or half a kalpa, enter the Stage of Joy (*pramuditābhūmi*)."
According to the *Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Adorned Necklace* (*Ābharaṇa-mūla-karma-sūtra*), regarding the stage of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*), that sūtra states:
"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] advances or retreats, they mostly remain in the sixth abiding while desiring to enter the seventh abiding."

Why is this? If a son of good family practices the six perfections for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas and thereby enters the seventh stage (*vihāra*), then from the first stage through the sixth, if he cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā* so that right contemplation manifests before him, and furthermore encounters the protection and mindfulness of various Buddhas and bodhisattvas who are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he will immediately attain the seventh stage and never again fall back.

From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and prior, it is called the "stage of regression" (*hānabhāgīya*); if sentient beings are born there and enter the seventh stage, they are named "non-regressive" (*avaivartika*), for this is certain, as at that time their long-term cultivation of conditions is powerful.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: because they lack the seven conditions for retrogression, all those born [in that state] are non-retrogressive.
First, the five factors of retrogression do not exist. As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"First, chronic illness; and so forth.
2. Traveling far; 3. Constantly reciting and practicing the scriptural teachings;
4. Constantly attending to worldly affairs.
Fifth, constantly reconciling disputes.
These five causes and conditions cause the mind to become weary; they are called the five factors of decline.

Second, having a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas, making offerings to the Buddhas, listening to the Dharma, and attending upon superior persons—thus practicing the path for a long duration—is called non-retrogression.

Third, because there are no women, there is no deluded craving of lustful desire; rather, when encountering the objects of the six sense-fields through seeing, hearing, touching, or cognizing, the mind remains unstained and gives rise to the bodhicitta. Because there is thus no condition for stained attachment, this is called "non-retrogression."
Fourth, because there is no unwholesomeness and nothing contrary to one's aspirations, one does not regress.

Fifth, because there are no evil friends and one constantly beholds the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*), the mind is free from pride and indolence; thus, through reverent practice, the mind does not regress.
Sixth, by the power of that Buddha’s vows, one does not regress.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings who, having been born in my land, do not undergo rebirth in the evil realms until they attain Buddhahood—except for those instances where such birth is manifested for pedagogical purposes—if this were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"If a person wishes to attain the stage of non-retrogression in their present body, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā and should recite the name of the Buddha Amitābha of the West."
Seventh, one does not regress for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There are two kinds of *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive):"
First, those who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

second, those who have not yet attained it—namely, sentient beings with physical bodies subject to birth and death whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not yet severed. Because the Buddha knows that such persons will certainly sever them in the future, and for the benefit of others, the Tathāgata also grants the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that those bodhisattvas are *avaivartika*.

The Tathāgata Śākyamuni also knows that we sentient beings, having been born there, will certainly not regress; therefore, he bestows this prediction from afar, which is also called "non-regression," and thus it is said that they are all *avaivartika*.

Why is this? If one will make a vow, it refers to the future; making a vow in the future means in a future life.
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are sons of good family who possess faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land. This next section explains the fourth exhortation to be born [there].
"If you all believe my words, you should make a vow to be born in that land.
Next follows the fifth great section, "The Rare Occurrence as Described by Others," which has four parts:
first, their praise;...
Second, marveling at his ability to endure;
third, wondering at his attainment of the supreme fruit;
fourth, praising the bestowal of the secret method.
The Sūtra says:
"Śāriputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable merits of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas proclaim my own inconceivable merits. This next section explains the first point: that praise.
I praise the Buddhas of the six directions who can serve as true witnesses for sentient beings; because of this, the minds of sentient beings become free from doubt.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata Amitābha draws them in through his great compassion; I specifically praise him, and that Buddha in turn praises me.
The Sūtra says:

"And he spoke these words: 'Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat, being able [to act] within the five corruptions of this Sahā world-system—the corruption of the eon, the corruption of views, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of sentient beings, and the corruption of life. This next section explains the second point of wonder: his ability to endure such conditions.
The *Svayaṃprati-jñā-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"Śākya" means "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren).
The *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* says:
The Muni is named "Quiescence" and is also called "Non-conceptuality.
The *Past Causes and Effects Sūtra* states:
it refers to the fulfillment of body, speech, and mind.
He is thus able to realize the quiescence of nirvāṇa, to realize non-conceptual wisdom, and to bring the merits of body, speech, and mind to fulfillment; therefore, he is called Śākyamuni.
One who is able to perform such an extremely difficult and rare feat is the Buddha, who endures amidst the five turbidities of evil.
As for the Sahā world, it is now translated as "Mixed Evil"; the *Svayaṃpratijñā-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"It is named the World of Endurance."
Paramārtha says:

"Kṣānti" is the name for the Brahmā King of this world-system; because he is able to endure the superior achievements of others without giving rise to jealousy, the realm is further named the Kṣānti World after its ruler.
Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"The sentient beings of this realm endure the three poisons and various afflictions; therefore, it is called the 'Land of Patience' (*Sahā-lokadhātu*).
Regarding the "five turbidities of the evil world," "five" refers to the number, and "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) refers to dregs.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"When ignorance is mixed with wisdom, it is termed 'turbidity' (*kaṣāya*).
Turbidity is the most inferior dregs and impurity; for example, when water, wine, ghee, or oil is pure and clear, the clarity remains above while the turbid dregs settle below."

When sentient beings first arise at the beginning of a kalpa, people can enjoy long lifespans, and their clothing and food are refined and excellent; their afflictions are slight and their various views are thin and weak; their physical forms are upright and handsome, and they are filial, compassionate, and respectful; being free from the five impurities, this is called "purity."

When the end of the kalpa is approaching, the times are evil, lifespans are short, afflictions are heavy and thick, and various views are deep-seated; people act with rebellion and lack compassion. Because these five impurities exist, they are called "turbidities."
The meaning of this "dregs" (kaṣāya) is explained extensively in a separate chapter; here, the names are briefly defined.
First, regarding the "dregs of the eon" (kalpa-kaṣāya): "eon" (kalpa) refers to time.
As the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:

Because sentient beings possess internal evil, there arise externally the three types of calamities: famine, pestilence, and warfare; when these three kalpas arise, they are termed the "kalpa-turbidity" (kalpa-kaṣāya).

The famine lasted for seven years, the disease for seven months, and the sword for seven days; although the durations were unequal, the death of the multitude was of one kind, and in each successive kalpa, more than half of those who died perished.

If sentient beings today give even a single morsel of food to the Sangha, they will not encounter the kalpa of famine; if they give even a single pill of medicine to the Sangha or to the poor and sick, they will not encounter the kalpa of disease; and if they practice the precept of non-killing and give rise to a mind of compassion, they will not encounter the kalpa of weapons.

Regarding these three kalpas, famine occurs first, followed by weapons, with disease in between; however, they do not occur in immediate succession, but rather in sequence. That is to say, at the conclusion of one *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor kalpa), there is a kalpa of famine; next, at the conclusion of another *kṣudra-kalpa*, there is a kalpa of disease; and finally, at the conclusion of yet another *kṣudra-kalpa*, there is a kalpa of weapons.
When these three calamities arise during the kalpa, it must be at a time when human lifespan is ten years; therefore, it is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Second is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): "view" refers to the five views; because they are sought through false wisdom and interpreted with a perverted mind, they are termed the turbidity of views.
The *Śīla-sūtra* states:

"As it is now, sentient beings perceive what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma; they proclaim what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma and what is the Dharma to be not the Dharma. Through such incorrect views, they give rise to false discrimination, destroying the True Dharma and increasing false teachings. Because they cause others to practice accordingly, this is called the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*)."
The third is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). This refers to the three poisons residing within the mind, which cause the mind to give rise to afflictions and create various evil karmas.

As the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "Because of afflictions, sentient beings create various evil karmas and amass evil implements—namely, weapons such as swords and spears used to harm sentient beings—all of which are termed the turbidity of afflictions."

Regarding the fourth, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): they arise by grasping at conventional name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Since name-and-form are not unitary, it is through the provisional aggregation of many dharmas that they are designated as "sentient beings."

Yet sentient beings forget kindness and turn their backs on righteousness; they are arrogant, deceitful, and fail to cultivate the three trainings or the ten virtuous actions, instead frequently committing the ten non-virtues and the five heinous crimes.
As the *Sukṣmasīla-sūtra* states:
"To cause sentient beings to be unable to provide filial support, to not respect teachers and elders, and to not perform virtuous deeds is called the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*)."

The fifth is the corruption of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). This refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—neither material nor mental—which is obtained as a karmic retribution for a single period of existence; this is called the corruption of lifespan.
If one cultivates wholesome karma, the life-faculty obtained will be long-lasting, perhaps eighty thousand years;
however, because sentient beings frequently engage in killing, stealing, and harming life, the conditions of their karma do not fulfill even a hundred years.
As the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"The lifespan of human beings gradually diminishes until it reaches ten years; at that point, one is immediately old and immediately dead. This is called the turbidity of life.
Thus, they are known as the five turbidities."
What is called "the Middle" refers to Śākyamuni appearing within the five turbidities.
The Sūtra says:
"He attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This next section explains the third point: the marvel of ascending to the supreme fruit.
It is truly marvelous that, amidst this evil age, in this evil place, and among these evil sentient beings, he is able to endure all manner of evils and attain Bodhi.
The Sūtra says:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches this Dharma which is difficult for all the world to believe. This constitutes the fourth explanation, praising the bestowal of the secret Dharma.

The "Dharma difficult for all the world to believe" refers to the fact that by recollecting the Buddha for even one day up to seven days, one immediately extracts oneself from the dregs of defilement and ascends to a pure realm; because this subtle cause results in such a manifest fruit, it is difficult for worldly sentiments to believe, and people fear these are merely the Tathāgata’s words used to guide and attract others—hence it is called a Dharma difficult to believe.
From here below begins the sixth major section, "A Personal Account of the Great Difficulty.
This text is divided into four parts:
first, revealing the causes for the difficulty of practice;
Second, revealing the fruit that is difficult to attain;
third, expounding the Dharma that is difficult to believe;
fourth, concluding that it is extremely difficult [to encounter].
The Sūtra says:

"Śāriputra! You should know that I perform these difficult tasks in this world of five turbidities; indeed, this is most difficult. In explaining this self-narration of the extreme difficulty, there are four phrases:
1. "I, amidst the five turbidities," and so forth, describes the defiled realm;
2. "Attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," describes the realization of the supreme fruit;
3. "Expounding [the Dharma] for all sentient beings," and so forth, describes the bestowal of secret methods.
"This is what is most difficult" concludes the three matters previously mentioned that were difficult to perform yet were accomplished.
From here below is the third section, clarifying the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) portion, which is the section on "receiving and practicing according to the teaching."
The text has three parts:
first, the completion of the teaching; second, the completion of what was heard; and third, receiving it with joy and upon the crown of the head.
The Sūtra says:

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
The commentary states:
"The Buddha has finished preaching the sutra" is the narration of the compilers, indicating that the speaker’s discourse is complete.
"The Elder [Ānanda] and others" refers to the fact that what was heard is fully recorded.
Having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the sutra, they immediately received it with joy and reverence.
Regarding the phrase "all worlds," since worldly things are not singular, it is said to be "all."
The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra: Sūryagarbha-parivarta* states:
"There are three worlds in the world:
first, the world of sentient beings, which refers to the various classes within the six destinies;"
2. The receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), which refers to the forty dwelling places within the three realms;
3. The world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*), which refers to the five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).
Why are these called "worlds" (*loka*)?
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
"Because it is precarious, fragile, and subject to decay, it is called the 'world' (*loka*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The devas are named "Lamp-Light" (*Dīpa-prabhā*) and also called "Radiance" (*Prabhā*). Because their radiance can dispel darkness and constitute a great illumination, they are called devas.

Furthermore, they are called devas because they are auspicious; they are called humans (*nara*) because they possess abundant benevolence and righteousness. One who possesses faith and possesses abundant benevolence and righteousness is thus called a human.
The *Mahādharmanirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Asuras are called 'Non-Gods' (*asura*); because they are not gods, they are named asuras.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) should include, by extension, the nāgas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, and others, which are omitted here for brevity.
Regarding "joyful" (*pramuditā*): because the mind is joyful and the body is pleased, it is called "joyful," as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"the mind is joyful and the body is pleased.
Furthermore, the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra-śāstra* states:
Possessing the three purities is called "joy":
first, the purity of the speaker, meaning that the Buddha is the Omniscient One who universally expounds for all sentient beings the complete and stainless Dharma-treasury of the sudden teaching;

second, the purity of what is spoken, meaning that the principle and the teaching correspond, and the words and meanings are compliant and non-contradictory, such that by relying upon them one attains liberation.

Third, the purity of the recipient: this refers to one who, having received [the teaching], acts with sincerity and faith, and does not give rise to disparagement or slander. Because these three meanings are present, it is called "joyful.

Furthermore, the expansion of the countenance is called "joy" (*huan*), and the delight of the spirit is called "rejoicing" (*xi*). Hearing it without slandering is termed "faith"; internalizing it within the mind is termed "receiving" (*shou*). Therefore, it is said: "joyfully and with faith, one receives."
Colophon: Transmitted by the practice lineage; transmitted by the practice lineage in the final age.

After the commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* was completed, a postscript states: "On the ninth day of the ninth month of the seventh year of the Dazhong era, the Venerable Changle of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou relinquished this to Zhen."

Colophon to the Commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*: Since Master Kumārajīva translated the *Amitābha Sūtra*, there have been no fewer than several dozen masters from successive dynasties who composed commentaries and records upon it; indeed, this tradition has been most flourishing!
The Master Ci'en Ji composed two works:
one titled the *Tongzan Shu* (Commentary on the General Praise) and the other simply titled the *Shu* (Commentary).

These two commentaries complement each other with varying degrees of detail, illuminating the meaning of the sutra like two lamps in a single room; their combined light makes the objects they reveal even more distinct. How could one of them possibly be discarded?

I have previously read the *Changxi lu* and observed the citations made by the Master Chanji; from these, I learned that in addition to the *Tongzan*, there was also a *Shu* (Commentary), which I deeply regret not being transmitted to the present day.

One day, while conversing with the two masters Zhiji and Huiyue, as well as Linsui, the topic happened to turn to this matter; I learned that it still existed within those collections. Consequently, I requested the two masters to transcribe a copy for me, which I then roughly edited and stored in a casket.

Recently, someone carved this work into printing blocks to share it with like-minded companions and stored the plates in the library at Huading Peak. As I am not ashamed of my own humble and clumsy efforts, I have briefly recounted the origins and circumstances of how I obtained this book to serve as a postscript to its end.
